heroText: Dakar is Senegal's vibrant Atlantic capital, built on a peninsula where colonial-era streets meet surf beaches and bustling markets. First-time visitors should take the ferry to Île de Gorée and its House of Slaves memorial, photograph the towering African Renaissance Monument, and browse fabrics and crafts at Marché Sandaga. Blaise Diagne International Airport sits outside the city at Diass, and Dakar's mix of nightlife, seafood and coastline makes it a natural hub for West African travel.

areas.name: Plateau
areas.text: Plateau is Dakar's colonial-era downtown, home to government buildings, banks and the ferry terminal for Île de Gorée, ideal for first-time visitors.

areas.name: Almadies
areas.text: Almadies is Dakar's upscale coastal district, lined with beach clubs, restaurants and nightlife near the continent's westernmost point.

areas.name: Ngor
areas.text: Ngor is a laid-back fishing village turned surf hangout, with a short pirogue ride to car-free Ngor Island just offshore.

areas.name: Yoff
areas.text: Yoff is a traditional Lebou fishing village along a long sandy beach, offering an authentic, lower-key base close to the airport road.

airports.name: Blaise Diagne International Airport (DSS)
airports.search: Blaise Diagne International Airport, Diass, Senegal
airports.text: Blaise Diagne International Airport sits about 45 kilometres southeast of central Dakar, so budget an hour or more for the transfer into the city.

airportTransfer.value: Compare road transfer time between Blaise Diagne International Airport (DSS) and central Dakar before choosing an airport-area or city-centre hotel.

stayOverview: Base in Plateau for an easy first stay near ministries, markets and the Gorée ferry, or choose Almadies for beach clubs and Dakar's best restaurants. Ngor suits surfers and relaxed island-hopping, while Yoff offers an authentic fishing-village base near the airport road.
hotelIntro: Dakar hotel choice depends on priorities: Plateau suits first-time visitors wanting downtown sights and the Gorée ferry within reach, Almadies suits beach and nightlife stays, and Ngor or Yoff suit travelers wanting a quieter, more local coastal base.
rentalCars: A rental car helps for day trips to Lac Rose or the airport at Diass, though taxis and ride-hailing cover Dakar's city centre and beaches easily.

travelTips.title: Best base
travelTips.text: Choose Plateau for downtown sights and the Gorée ferry, or Almadies for beach clubs and Dakar's liveliest restaurant scene.

travelTips.title: Airport distance
travelTips.text: Allow extra time for the roughly hour-long transfer from Blaise Diagne International Airport, which sits well outside the city centre.

travelTips.title: Gorée ferry
travelTips.text: Book the Île de Gorée ferry a day ahead in high season and arrive early, since queues build quickly at the Plateau terminal.

travelTips.title: Bargaining and cash
travelTips.text: Carry West African CFA francs for markets and negotiate prices at Marché Sandaga and Kermel, where bargaining is expected.

nearbyIdeas.label: Nature
nearbyIdeas.text: Lac Rose, also called Lake Retba, turns a striking pink from algae and salt, a popular half-day trip northeast of Dakar.

nearbyIdeas.name: Île de Ngor
nearbyIdeas.label: Beach
nearbyIdeas.text: Île de Ngor is a tiny car-free island reached by pirogue from Ngor village, good for a relaxed beach afternoon and surf breaks.

nearbyIdeas.text: Saly is Senegal's main beach resort strip south of Dakar, worth a longer stay for golf, watersports and all-inclusive hotels.

history.text: Peaceful contact was finally opened in 1456 by Diogo Gomes, and the bay was subsequently referred to as the "Angra de Bezeguiche" (after the name of the local ruler).

history.label: 16th century
history.text: The bay of "Bezeguiche" would go on to serve as a critical stop for the Portuguese India Armadas of the early 16th century, where large fleets would routinely stop, both on their outward and.
The Portuguese founded a settlement on the island of Gorée (then known as the island of Bezeguiche or Palma), which by 1536 they began to use as a base for slave exportation.

history.label: 17th century
history.text: A new Lebou village, called Ndakaaru, was established directly across from Gorée in the 17th century to service the European trading factory with food and drinking water.
The island switched hands between the Portuguese and Dutch several more times before falling to the English under Admiral Robert Holmes on January 23, 1664, and finally to the French in 1677.

history.label: 1780s
history.text: The infamous "House of Slaves" was built at Gorée in 1776. Lebou Republic By the 1780s, Dakar was one of the largest towns in Cayor.
Traders from Gorée decided to move to the mainland, and a "factory" with warehouses was established in Rufisque in 1840.
In 1857, the French established a military post at Ndakaaru (which they called "Dakar") and annexed the Lebou Republic, though its institutions continued to function nominally.

The port facilities were improved with jetties, a telegraph line was established along the coast to Saint-Louis, and the Dakar-Saint-Louis railway was completed in 1885, at which point the city became an important base.
A second major railroad, the Dakar-Niger built from 1906 to 1923, linked Dakar to Bamako and consolidated the city's position at the head of France's West African empire.
In 1940, Dakar became involved in the Second World War when General de Gaulle, leader of the Free French Forces, sought to make the city the base of his resistance operations.
On 1 December 1944, French soldiers guarding the camp opened fire on the West African soldiers.

Accounts of the death toll range from around 35 (the official French account) to over 300 (army veterans active at the time). Independence Dakar was the capital of the short-lived Mali Federation from 1959.

history.label: Regional role
history.text: French trading firms established branch offices there, and industrial investments (mills, breweries, refineries, canneries) were attracted by its port and rail facilities.
